That depends on outcome trial results, expected over the next few years.
faq.q: Which siRNA drug will be first?

name: RNA Based Lp(a) Therapies
title: RNA Based Lp(a) Therapies
answer: RNA drugs stop the liver making apolipoprotein(a). Pelacarsen, an antisense drug, lowers Lp(a) by about 80 percent but failed its outcome trial; the siRNA drugs olpasiran, lepodisiran and zerlasiran lower it by more than 90 percent with dosing every few months or less often, and their outcome trials are still running.

sections.body: Percentage lowering is not proof of benefit. Judge these drugs by their outcome trials, safety and dosing, not by how far they push the number down.
sections.heading: What it means for patients

explainer:
Antisense oligonucleotides and small interfering RNAs both target the messenger RNA that carries the LPA gene's instructions, so less apolipoprotein(a) is made. They are attached to a sugar called GalNAc that steers them to liver cells, which allows small doses. Antisense drugs bind the RNA directly and are given monthly or so; siRNA drugs use the cell's own machinery to destroy the RNA and last much longer, every three to six months or possibly once a year.

These are not gene therapies: they do not change DNA, and their effect wears off unless dosing continues. The open questions are whether deeper lowering translates into fewer events, how long benefits take to appear, and whether rare side effects emerge in large, long trials.

developments.text: Reported phase 2 reductions: olpasiran more than 95 percent, lepodisiran 93.9 percent lasting over 12 months after one dose, zerlasiran 96.4 percent, pelacarsen about 80 percent.
Pelacarsen's Lp(a)HORIZON outcome trial did not meet its primary endpoint.
